That means that China's rising, America's in decline. And Trump says, "Yeah, he said he's declining, but declining under Biden, but now it's doing great under Trump." All this kind of stuff. Look, um I I think that um we lived back in the Cold War when I was growing up, we had two superpowers. The Americans thought the Soviets were much stronger superpower than they were. They thought their economy was much more robust than it actually was, but the world had different countries, and some of them aligned with the US, and some of them aligned with the Soviets. And that was clearest in Europe where you actually had the Berlin Wall. And if you were on one side, you had one political system, one economic system. You were on the other side, you had a very different life. And that defined a lot of who you were. The Soviet Union, I started my graduate school in 1989. And the Soviet Union collapses. The Berlin Wall comes down. So suddenly there's only one superpower, right? It's the United States. It's the new world order. And And we're going to win. So everyone's going to want to be like us, right? They're all going to integrate. And so you're going to reach out, and China joined the WTO, the World Trade Organization, and NATO expands, and the EU expands, and everyone's going to be allies. And then now people look at the world and they say, "Well, I mean, even if the US is the most powerful country, because the most importantly it has the reserve currency, the dollar that most people trade in, um and that provides a level of gravitational pull to the US, most people wouldn't say that the US acts like the global superpower. Because the US doesn't want to be the leader of everyone. Trump says it's the Monroe Doctrine. It's the Western Hemisphere. That's where America really wants to dominate. But Ukraine really far away. And so the Europeans should take care of that with the Russians or you know, Taiwan's really far away. And so that should be the Chinese and and the Japanese and all that. They should figure that out, right? So So Trump and and not just Trump, but previous American presidents have have increasingly acted as if some of the core precepts [snorts] of superpower leadership, which was for the Americans it was we're going to be the sheriff, right? We're going to be the architect of global trade, and we're going to promote universalist values, just like we did after World War II, the United Nations. And that's what a superpower is. Well, the Americans aren't doing that anymore. So, today, even if the US still has the global reserve currency, and it does, and the US has the biggest military, the only military that has global reach with bases all over the place, and it does, that's true, but the United States doesn't want to be the global sheriff, right? Um I'm saying that very clearly, wants other countries to do much more of their own lifting, take care of their own national security. US certainly doesn't want free trade. They're putting tariffs on that we haven't seen in almost 100 years on countries all over the world, including India, right? And they're not promoting global democracy and rule of law all over the world. The United States isn't even sure that it has an effective democracy itself. They're fighting internally over what America stands for. So, even if the United States is the most powerful country, and there are other countries that are increasing China is increa- creasingly powerful, and very competitive with the US on on technology, for example, very competitive in terms of commercial and trade relations with other countries around the world. More countries do more trade with China than with the United States, for example. China's a lot more people. India has even more people than China, right? Um so, there are lots of ways you can think about the power balance changing, but the most important thing is if the United States does not want to take leadership globally, then you can't say that the United States is a superpower. And that means that what's happening in the world is much more uncertain. It's much more volatile. And and I think the reason for that the reason for that is because you now have a misalignment >> Mhm. >> between the rules and the institutions and the architecture of how the world works and the balance of power, right? It's changed a lot. Not just because the Soviet Union collapsed, but also because Russia wasn't brought in. >> Yeah. >> And China was rising. And people said, "Okay, we'll bring China in, but what if we don't really trust China? What if China doesn't integrate with what we want?" India is rising. Okay, we'll bring India in, but what if we What if India doesn't want to really be our ally or our friend? And then the United States says, "Well, we don't want to do all of this stuff." So, those are the reasons why we have this huge uncertainty, what I would call a G0 world. Not G7, not G20, but an absence of global leadership and therefore a geopolitical recession. All right? Just like we have economic recessions, boom and bust cycles, we have geopolitical recessions, but they're much longer. They're much longer. They don't happen as frequently, and you don't necessarily recognize when you're in it. But here's the key point. Is it if you're in a geopolitical recession, where you don't have global leadership, there are only three ways out. Only three. >> What are they? >> One is that you take the institutions and the rules of the road that you didn't used to believe in as much and you make them stronger. The second is you invest in them. The second is you build new institutions and architecture that better reflects what people need and the new balance of power today. >> Yeah. >> The third is you go to war. That's it. There are no other choices. There's a fourth, actually. There's a fourth. The fourth is you ignore it. You pretend that there's no geopolitical recession and you act as if everything is fine, which by the way, the Europeans had been doing for a long time until the Russians punched them in the face, right? You can pretend. Number four is a bad strategy, right? But number three, the first three, we are doing the first three, right? I mean, you see that like the Europeans are investing more in Europe because they know they need to. Why? Most of the those leaders who are the global leaders on the global stage would say the American government is still the leader. I mean, the the NRA, the National Rifle Association, is not a company, but it is a special interest. The trial lawyers or the teachers union or AIPAC, those are not companies, but they are special interests. Not because America is truly controlled by by the corporates, but because the role of money is making them feel these leaders don't represent me, they represent the big money. Big piece of that can't trust the Americans need better relations there. Europeans spending much more on defense, right? That's not happening. They are too small, too diffuse, not coordinated, don't share enough interests. But all of the middle powers are engaging in the same hedging strategy to reduce at the margins their exposure. And the second thing that happens is you invest more in your own resilience. So if you're a Gulf state and you know you can't count on the Americans for the Strait of Hormuz, you need to build out your security, your defense. If you're the Europeans and you can't count on the Americans for Ukraine, you've got to spend a lot more on your own defense. The Japanese are doing the same thing. But, what you can't do is pretend that reality doesn't exist. And reality is that the United States is still the most powerful country. >> Yeah. >> The United States is still the most powerful defense capability.
